title: Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor encephalitis presenting with acute psychosis in a preteenage girl: a case report
case_prompt:
An 11-year-old previously healthy girl was admitted with alternating confusion and agitation. Twelve days earlier, she had a 3-day history of headaches, nausea, and sleepiness, followed by behavioral changes over one week, including poor school performance, reduced food intake, disturbed sleep, excessive and unintelligible speech focused on her clothes, panic episodes possibly due to visual hallucinations, and escalating agitation. A cranial MRI performed one week before admission was normal, and she was diagnosed with an acute psychotic episode and started on olanzapine.

On admission, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable with normal respiratory function. Neurologic examination showed stupor with agitation, fluctuating consciousness with loss of speech and eye contact, limb dyskinesias, urinary incontinence, and self-harm behaviors (lip biting, head banging). During hospitalization, she had brief lucid intervals interrupted by visual and auditory hallucinations; frequent agitation was followed by dystonia of the left leg, lower jaw movements, rhythmic tongue thrusting, chewing motions, teeth grinding, and lip biting. She experienced focal seizures of either side, and some episodes featured a transient urticarial-like rash and mild fever (37–37.7 °C).

An electroencephalogram demonstrated right-side slowing without epileptiform discharges. Repeat cranial MRI was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 5 WBC/µL and the presence of oligoclonal bands; protein concentration was normal. PCR assays for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 were negative, and serologic tests for adenovirus, enterovirus, cytomegalovirus, measles, rubella, toxoplasma, and mycoplasma were negative. Toxicology screens on blood and urine were unremarkable. No evidence of metabolic disorders, including Wilson’s disease and porphyria, was identified. Autoimmune screening revealed negative anti-nuclear antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies, and anti-Sm nuclear antigen.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Primary psychiatric disorder considered — “she was diagnosed with an acute psychotic episode and prescribed olanzapine” but progression with neurologic signs argued against a pure psychiatric cause.  
2. HSV encephalitis excluded — “PCR for herpes simplex viruses (HSV-1,2)…were negative.”  
3. Other viral encephalitides excluded — “negative serology for viruses (adenovirus, enterovirus, cytomegalovirus, measles and rubella), toxoplasma, and mycoplasma.”  
4. Toxic etiology ruled out — “Toxicology tests on blood and urine were negative.”  
5. Metabolic causes excluded — “No evidence was found for possible metabolic causes, including Wilson’s disease and porphyria.”  
6. Systemic lupus erythematosus excluded — “Negative anti-nuclear antibodies, antiphospholipid antibody, normal titer of anti–DNA antibody to native DNA and absence of antibody to Sm nuclear antigen excluded systemic lupus erythematosus.”  
7. Anti-NMDAR encephalitis confirmed — “Anti-NMDAR antibodies were revealed on immunohistochemistry in her serum and CSF.”
